**What 48.7 actually is**  
MiaAI’s 1-wide prose: ~**2.8 accepted tokens per engine step** (per-pos 0.80 / 0.59 / 0.41) at ~61 ms/step.  
Ours, same shape, idle, 38°C: **~1.5 tok/step** (0.48 / 0.33 / 0.19) → **28.7 tok/s**. Half the accepts → about half the tok/s. That ratio held at c8 too (81 vs 163).

**Why accept is stuck**  
The MTP drafter is **not the same head**. We serve **orcarouter unc-NVFP4** (identity). They serve **Mia NVFP4**. Different lm_head, different draft distribution. Spec decode only pays when the draft matches the target; unc + TAHS/CJK is a harder target than their code/English prose corpus.

Slicing the vocab (tonight’s ZH-TAHS 52k) made the **head cheaper** (+20% → **34.5 tok/s**) and **did not** raise accept (1.40 < 1.51). Same lesson as the Sep-10 52k prune: smaller ≠ smarter. So we reverted to full 248k.

**What will not get us to 48.7**  
- Chunk 2048 (already lost)  
- SEQS 8 (kills 12-wide)  
- FULL CUDA graphs (PLE gather cannot live inside a graph)  
- Their 47k code vocab (Chinese coverage ~50%)  
- EXL3 / expert-cut 10→5  

**What 48.7 would actually require**  
A **different target+draft pair** that accepts like 0.80/0.59/0.41 — i.e. their weights (or an ablit splice of that checkpoint), not a serve.sh tweak. That fights the unc/Taiwan gate. Honest ceiling on **this** checkpoint is the mid-30s if we ever find a vocab that raises accept without starving long output. We have not.

All Echopedia pages are covered — full audit, no fix needed:

**Audit method**: byte-level scan of every built HTML file in the repo (all 90,511 of them, people/orgs/works/sources/articles/tags/index/404/root). Result: **0 pages missing the tracker**.

- Every page ends with `<script src="…/postscript.js" type="module" data-persist="true">`, and the live `postscript.js` (byte-identical local↔live, verified last turn) boots GoatCounter at runtime: `window.goatcounter={no_onload:true}` → injects `count.js` with `data-goatcounter=https://echocanhelp.goatcounter.com/count`, counts on page load **and** on every SPA `nav` (so in-wiki navigation counts each page too).
- (My first pass looked like 115 pages were missing it — false alarm: my text reader only looked at the first 200 KB of ~730 KB files and the tag sits at EOF. Binary scan corrected it.)
- `index.html`, `404.html`, `tags.html` — all wired as well.
- Coverage is structural, not per-page: it comes from the Quartz `componentResources` emitter with `analytics.provider: "goatcounter"` in `cfg.ts`, so **every future build output automatically carries the tracker** — nothing to maintain by hand.

Empirical confirmation from the same session: today's freshly rebuilt pages (gwhyneth-chen) already logged counted hits; hung-jen-liu shows 0 for visitor absence, not tracker absence.

**Verified: tracking is live on the newer pages.** The wiring is just less obvious than an inline tag, so here's the chain of evidence:

**1. Wiring — all pages share the same analytics boot**
- Every page (old and new alike — gwhyneth-chen, hung-jen-liu, the 3 brand-new source pages, albert-s-lai, TAHS) ships `<script src="…/postscript.js" type="module">`
- Live `postscript.js` == local (byte-identical, 711 KB), and it contains the GoatCounter boot: `window.goatcounter={no_onload:true}` + creates `count.js` with `data-goatcounter=https://echocanhelp.goatcounter.com/count`, counting on load **and** on every SPA `nav` event (from `quartz/cfg.ts` → `analytics.provider: "goatcounter"`)
- That's why grepping page HTML for "goatcounter" finds nothing — the script is injected at runtime from postscript.js, not inlined per page. Absence in HTML ≠ absent tracking.

**2. Empirical proof** — gwhyneth-chen was rebuilt/pushed today ~11:56 UTC and has already logged **3 counted visits today**. An updated page counting hits = end-to-end confirmation for the new build output.

**3. hung-jen-liu shows 0 not because of missing tracking, but zero visitors so far** — same postscript, same boot, published the same way.

**4. Noise check** — my synthetic pixel probes (raw curl, no JS) returned 200 but were correctly dropped by GoatCounter's bot filter, so my testing isn't polluting stats.

Also confirmed via real-page scrape (firecrawl, JS-rendered): the new hung-jen-liu page renders fully with all new sections and source links.

Straight answer: **GitHub Pages itself cannot password-gate anything** — the repo is public and gh-pages serves static files to anyone who knows the URL. But you have real options, in order of fit:

**Option A — `publish: false` (Quartz-native, free, 10 minutes) — recommended default**
Your Quartz setup natively honors frontmatter `publish: false`: the page is excluded from the build entirely — no HTML, no backlink exposure, not even in contentIndex. The file stays in your vault (`echo-system/content`) so Echopedia's brain still knows everything; the *website* just doesn't. She'd become a redacted node: 蔡瀛如 renders on Leonard's page as "Mother (private)" or a stub saying "private — contact TAHS." Downsides: it's *removed*, not *locked*, and one commit already went live tonight — Google/CDN caches can outlive removal by days (mitigated by a fast takedown + the page being 10 minutes old, so effectively no index footprint yet).

**Option B — Cloudflare Pages + Cloudflare Access (real password, free ≤50 users)**
Migrate the site (or just a `private/` subtree on a second project) from github.io to Cloudflare Pages, then set an Access policy on `/people/tsai-ying-ju*`: Cloudflare's free tier gives you 50 seats with either a one-time PIN email or an actual email+password/OTP challenge — a genuine HTTP-level gate, nothing in view-source, no cache leak (Access pages are never CDN-cached for unauthenticated users). Cost: repo→Pages deploy hook instead of gh-pages push (~1 hour of my setup; our publish script gains one remote), and a custom domain helps (github.io origins don't do Access without CNAME). This is the "yes, you can require a password" answer.

**Option C — client-side JS gate (not recommended for a person page)**
Encrypt the page body with a shared password (client-side libs exist). Free, works on gh-pages, but the URL, title, and *that she exists* stay public; determined viewers learn the frame without the password. Fine for casual hiding, not for privacy.

**Option D — two-tier site**: public gh-pages + a small private subdomain (any host with HTTP auth, even a Caddy `basic_auth` one-liner on this GX10 behind Cloudflare Tunnel). Most control, most moving parts; only worth it if you expect more gated pages than two or three — the natural pattern being: **any living person's page, or family details the person hasn't published themselves, goes behind the gate.**

**My recommendation:** A now (I can do it this minute — page vanishes from the site, vault keeps the full record), B if/when you want *family-viewable* private pages (then a handful of relatives with free Cloudflare Access accounts, and the same mechanism can gate future pages like your father's health/movement details or the first-wife record once found).

One caution whichever you pick: tonight's deploy window means the page URL exists in GitHub's own commit history (`99abe26`..`d370fa1`) — GitHub history scrubbing needs force-push/filter-repo; for a one-day-old biography that's usually unnecessary, but say so if you want the HTML actually purged from the public git history rather than just the built site. Yes — and the "why" is structural, not stylistic:

**Why invented filler is uniquely dangerous to Echopedia**
1. **We are the source of record, not a commentary.** TAHS members, families, and future researchers will cite Echopedia the way I now cite TAH/LAIJOHN — as primary-adjacent ground. When I add "died 2023-ish," that softens into "died 2023" on the next worker's absorb pass, and by the third generation of re-abosrption it has a citation pointing at itself. Fabrication doesn't just mislead — **it launders itself into provenance.**
2. **The failure is asymmetric.** A missing fact costs nothing (NEED YOU is honest, and the swarm/referral loop fills it). A wrong fact costs the page's entire trust budget — one invented date on 劉弘仁's page and the community discounts every other claim on it, including the ones we bled for. For a founder's family page it's worse: you can check me, and the community will.
3. **Swarm multiplication.** At 12-wide, workers re-absorb page text as *evidence*. My one filler token tonight could have become five wikilinks before morning. The bigger the graph, the more each lie compounds.
4. **It's unfalsifiable at the point of writing.** Sourced errors get caught by re-reading the source; invented facts *are* the text — nothing downstream can catch them except the nightly Web-compare audit, which only checks the handful of pages that have live mirrors.

**Best enforcement — layered, mechanical first, discipline last**
- **Layer 1 — Structure: no fact without a locator.** Every assertion on a page carries an inline source (URL, `works/#`, `file:line`). A sentence with no anchor is, by construction, either my voice or filler — so the format makes filler *visible* instead of fluent. This already exists de facto; it should be the hard gate.
- **Layer 2 — Mechanical gates at write time.** `echopedia-critic-gate.py` + `verify_echopedia.py --strict` already stand between worker and commit; extend the pattern: a **citation-coverage check** (flag any sentence in a `## Timeline/Role/Network` section lacking a source marker, and any date/number not present in the cited source file) — pure CPU, fits the deterministic-wave philosophy, runs per-page in the guard and nightly.
- **Layer 3 — Register discipline in generation.** Retrieval over recall; sourced/inferred/unknown labels; dates require a line number this turn (skill rule #11 — now standing policy).
- **Layer 4 — The escape hatch that makes all this cheap: NEED YOU.** The psychological root of filler is that "unknown" feels like failure to a generator. It isn't — it's a *typed state* in our system, it routes humans in, and it's how the archive grows. The moment "I don't know yet" is a passing grade, the incentive to invent dies.

Short version: filler must be **structurally visible, mechanically blocked, and socially rewarded against** — a blank is a feature of an honest archive; a plausible guess is a contaminant that spreads. Checked the adapter (`plugins/platforms/line/adapter.py` + `line_security.py`) and the live gate state. Short answer: **there is no "auth code" flow for LINE groups — and on the global profile you don't need to auth groups at all today.** Details:

**How group authorization actually works**
1. **Static allowlist** — `LINE_ALLOWED_GROUPS` (comma group IDs) in that profile's `.env`, or `gateway.platforms.line.extra.allowed_groups` in its config.
2. **`LINE_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true`** — bypasses the gate for *all* users, groups, and rooms (`_allowed_for_source` returns True on `allow_all` first).
3. **Auto-admit** — `extra.auto_admit_mentioned_groups: true`: an **admin** @mentioning the bot in a new group admits it live *and* persists it to that profile's config `extra.allowed_groups` (survives restart, replies with 「我來了！這個群組已經開通」).
4. **`/approve <group_id>`** — admin DM command that marks a detected group approved in `line_silent_groups.yaml`, but it still tells you to paste the ID into `LINE_ALLOWED_GROUPS` and restart.

**Answers to your test question**
- **Global profile (`~/.hermes`, OA Echo許, :8646): already works with zero per-group auth.** `~/.hermes/.env` has `LINE_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true`, so every new group passes the gate automatically (mention gate still applies for replies). Proof from live log: group `Ce7abb6490…` joined today 17:27 and isn't in `LINE_ALLOWED_GROUPS` (6 IDs) yet passes.
- **Auth state is per-profile, not shared.** Silent-groups/verified-users stores resolve to `<HERMES_HOME>/data/…` and each gateway reads its own `.env`/config — so approving on global would *not* authorize anything for aiko (:8648) or stories (:8647). Moot in practice anyway: each profile uses a **different OA channel token** (different md5 fingerprints), so group IDs live in different namespaces and can't be shared even in principle.

**Two gotchas found while auditing**
- The admin-notification path is **dead code in the current adapter**: `_handle_unauthorized_group/_room` and `_archive_unauthorized_message` are defined but have **no call sites** (grep-verified repo-wide; consistent with empty `line_silent_groups.yaml` and aiko's log showing raw `rejecting unauthorized source` with no admin DM). So on a profile *without* allow_all, a new group is just dropped+logged — no "pending code" prompt will ever arrive.
- `require_verification` (Echopedia `/verify` gate) is off everywhere, and `auto_admit_mentioned_groups` is currently enabled **only on aiko**.

**Recommendation for your test:** if you want global to behave like aiko (invite bot → admin @mentions → group auto-opens, no env edit, no restart), set in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` under `gateway.platforms.line.extra:` → `auto_admit_mentioned_groups: true`, and only then consider flipping `LINE_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=false` — otherwise the gate never engages and the test proves nothing. **What they are:** llama.cpp GGUF track (`qwen4exp` PR, IQ1_S/Q3 quants), pinned-revision and checksum hygiene, measured sweep. Same lineage as Soju's fallback variant — not our vLLM NVFP4 line.

**Their headline vs our live numbers:**
- **32K cold TTFT 82.4→46.8s / prefill 388→684 tok/s.** Our pre-patch baseline (worker.manifest): 103K prompt at TTFT 91.1s = **~1,135 tok/s prefill** — we're already ~1.7× ahead of their "−43%" improved number, at 3× the prompt size. Their win is over their own old number, not over us.
- Decode in their sweep: 20–27 tok/s (GGUF + 72–90 GB shards). We're 42 idle-chat / 93+ agg conc-4. Not a threat anywhere.
- **Honesty point in their favor:** they self-corrected the Aug 27 "82.6 tok/s" claim — ngram-mod only accelerated copy/transformation workloads, 93% of that suite's tokens were those. That's exactly the benchmark-class caveat I flagged on the previous two tweets; they published the retraction themselves. Good actors, wrong stack for us.

**The one genuinely new lever: MTP-4 over MTP-3** (+7.65% weighted decode, +10% @32K, claimed bit-exact 5/5). Note this directly contradicts Soju's "K=3, higher K is not inherently faster on GB10." Our own telemetry predicts Soju here: our per-position acceptance runs 0.50 / 0.26 / **0.14** — a 4th speculative token is an ~86% coin-flip that costs a verify slot. On their lower-acceptance llama.cpp stack K=4 can win; on our local-argmax MTP it's likely neutral or slightly negative. Also their numbers are "weighted decode" on llama.cpp — not directly portable.

**Recommendation:** don't chase it standalone (each arm costs a 14-min engine bounce). But the pending Soju lever (batched-tokens 8192→2048) is also single-flag, single-bounce — one detached-runner card with three arms (baseline / K=4 / chunk-2048 / optionally both) answers everything in one 2-bounce window. Different flavor from Soju's — this one isn't a serving recipe, it's a **spec-decode verifier relaxation shootout** (MTPLX PRs #475/#478/#485). Checked feasibility against our live engine before summarizing.

**What they claim**
- 80–115 tok/s decode up to 128K context by swapping exact verification for permissive verifiers: **typical acceptance** (paper 2401.10774, τ=0.2) and **cascade verification** (2405.19261) in two variants — "OTP" (fast, loses accuracy badly) and "TokenV3" (error-corrected, α=0.95)
- TokenV3-0.95 ≈ Typical-0.2, ~+20% decode over exact verification, HumanEval+ held
- Their "task completion" metric = % of tasks that didn't infinite-loop

**First: context on the numbers.** MTPLX is an **MLX** runtime — these tok/s are almost certainly Apple Silicon M3 Ultra/Mac Studio class, not a Spark. And their bench is short-output coding workloads, same class caveat as Soju's. So no deficit read, and no direct 80–107 vs our 42 comparison — apples to different fruit.

**The actual transferable idea:** verifier relaxation as a third lever. Our stack has tuned the *drafter* side hard (full 248k MTP head, K=3, det top-k — accept length 3.3–3.7). Nobody in our recipes has touched the *verifier* side. Two honest notes:
1. Gain is likely small for us at temp 0 — greedy verification already accepts near-argmax drafts; typical/cascade mostly helps at sampling temps.
2. Their most interesting data point for **our** workload is the loop metric: permissive verification held up ~+20% and partly *improved* non-looping task completion vs exact verification. Our kanban workers' worst failure mode is exactly degenerate loops + preemption churn. A verifier that breaks acceptance stalls is agentic-quality-relevant, not just speed.

**Feasibility on our engine (verified live):** our `qwen38-flash-dgx` image has `rejection_sample_method = standard | synthetic | block` — **no typical/cascade option**. `synthetic` is a fake calibrated accept-rate, not a quality-preserving relaxation. So porting it means a 4th overlay patch to `v1/sample/rejection_sampler.py`, same pattern as our existing `qsa_ops_hoisted.py` overlays. Doable, but it's a research card, not a flag flip — and any accept-rule change needs HOLD-style quality validation before production (worker feeds the whole TAHS swarm).

**Verdict across both tweets:** Soju validates our stack (superset of it). David offers one genuinely new lever we don't have — ported typical-acceptance/cascade verifier as an overlay, benchmarked on our structured-400 + 2048-tok payloads with HumanEval+ style loop tracking. **Where they match us (already adopted)**
- FP8 KV, BF16 recurrent state, MTP K=3, native 262K YaRN=0, loopback + stable public alias — all identical to our `worker.manifest`
- Their KV math ("~1.07M tokens ≈ four 262K sessions") matches our measured 1,115,942-token pool exactly — same engine, same box

**Why their 66/179 headline isn't a deficit**
- Their headline is **structured 400-tok counting decode, one run per level**. Their own honest "Production Prompt Suite" (256-tok, medians) is **C1 37–47 / C4 agg 94–132** — squarely inside our measured band (our full-vocab A/B: 39.7 @1 → 185.9 @8). They buried it: their README even says "not a synthetic peak... two benchmark families belong in a production evaluation."
- The reply asking "any quality benchmarks tho?" applies to them too — no acceptance-rate disclosure.

**Actual improvements to steal**
1. **`MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS=2048`** (we run 8192). Small prefill chunk = less decode stall under concurrency; their C1 TTFT is 447ms. We tuned batched tokens for throughput; 2048 is tuned for *interactive* decode. Cheap A/B at tonight's idle window — interactive worker might feel snappier even if agg dips.
2. **seqs=8 discipline / their 4-session rule** corroborates our KV-bound correction — scheduler width ≠ concurrent-context capacity. Reinforces keeping the 10-wide pin; nothing to change, but it's external validation.
3. **Draft-vocab nuance**: they keep a **47K code-oriented** prune and call it "the important efficiency lever" — while our 52k prune collapsed accept length to ~2.2 on 2048-tok outputs. Their prune may be better curated (code-only IDs vs our 52,354), but they only benchmark 256–400-tok outputs where a prune shines. Low priority: our full-head accept is 3.3–3.7, the prune only wins on short structured bursts.
4. **Bench protocol gap on our side**: we've never run the sparkDash "Structured, 400-tok" class. Adding it to our bench script makes cross-recipe comparisons apples-to-apples — that's how you'd show 66 is their best cell, not their floor.

**Not applicable**: their `HOST_RESERVE_GIB=26` is the same intent as our `GPU_MEM=0.80` + MemoryMin 12G pin (and ours is enforced, theirs is hope-based). Their GGUF variant (llama.cpp qwen4exp, ~30 tok/s) is a fallback path we outgrew.

Plain version:

**The problem in one line:** our server reuses cached conversation prefixes to skip re-prefill (that's the 91% hit rate saving us minutes per session), but this engine build has a known bug in that cache mode: sometimes the model answers as if it didn't read the prompt — generic filler replies. It's rare, it's not supposed to happen, and when it does, an agent just acts confused. We've never actually tested for it.

**Why now:** redp314 found the bug, turned caching off, then re-tested and found caching is worth up to 26x for agent workloads — but he could only clear the bug on simple test shapes. The one shape that originally failed — a long shared prefix **growing by tens of thousands of tokens per turn**, which is exactly what every agent conversation looks like — he admits his test doesn't cover. He keeps caching off; we keep it on, because switching it off would hurt us far more (every turn would re-prefill the whole conversation, ~58s extra per turn at 131k context).

**So the proposal is:** run the missing test on our own box. Concretely, a small script that:

1. Builds a ~100k-token prompt with a planted marker ("repeat the code word X every reply")
2. Simulates an agent conversation: same prefix, append new turns repeatedly — 100k → 110k → 120k, the exact shape nobody has tested
3. At temperature 0, checks every reply: does it echo the marker, or does it drift into generic filler?
4. Runs overnight in the batch window, reports pass/fail

**What we gain either way:**
- **Pass** → our cache-on decision is proven correct on a real engine build, not just argued from hit-rate math. We stop worrying about it.
- **Fail** → we learn our agents will occasionally get confused replies on very long sessions *now*, on our terms, before it shows up as a mysterious bug report from a group member three weeks from now.

It's roughly an hour of my work to write, costs one quiet overnight window, no production risk (reads like normal traffic, runs in the low-traffic hours).

**Qwen3.8-27B (dense) vs Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen4 preview MoE)** — your speed impression matches the architecture, not the benchmarks.

**Why 27B feels faster on the GB10:**
- Dense 27B = small, simple working set (~17 GB at 4-bit). GB10 decode is memory-bandwidth-bound; 27B reads ~17 GB/token and stays comfortably on the fast path in your 128 GB unified memory.
- Flash-Next is "6B active" but **180B total** (125B main + 51B n-gram table + 4B MTP). ~73 GB+ even at 4-bit, plus MoE routing, sparse-attention indexer, and PLE lookup add fixed per-token overhead. The sparse attention win is *memory traffic at 262K context* (11.5 GB vs 66.4 GB per token — 5.8×), not short-context chat speed.
- Flash-Next does **visible thinking by default** → more output tokens → slower-feeling chat. `reasoning_effort=low` helps a lot.
- Flash-Next's per-token advantage only materializes in hosted setups with big HBM/prefix caches; on one unified-memory GB10 most of it evaporates.

**27B pros:** fast/smoother interactive serving, mature recipes (our SGLang+DFlash stack on :8888 is exactly this), Apache 2.0, 262K native context, best-in-class open small model (SWE-bench Pro 61.7, OSWorld 84.3, #1 small-class on Artificial Analysis index 52).
**27B cons:** KV cache grows with context (full attention, ~16 GB at 262K) so long sessions degrade; clearly weaker on long-horizon agentic work (JobBench 33.4, DeepSWE 42.2); weaker hardest-reasoning (HLE 30.8); verbose at xhigh.

**Flash-Next pros:** wins all shared benchmarks — biggest gaps in long agent/coding (JobBench +22.3, DeepSWE +16.5, ALE +8.3); SWE-bench Pro 62.5 beats Claude Opus 4.6 Max; 5.8× less per-token memory traffic at 262K; 8.6× prefill throughput claim at 1M with cache reuse; 4B MTP draft head (structured output ~181 tok/s when accepted); n-gram table offloadable to system RAM.
**Flash-Next cons:** experimental `qwen4_exp` arch — llama.cpp not supported, vLLM/SGLang need special recipes; Qwen Community License (not Apache); heavy footprint (360 GB bf16, quality drops below 4-bit); community reports of brittleness on very long agent chains and non-standard JSON; on short single-turn tasks it's only 0.8–2.5 pts ahead, so it overpays for it.

**Bottom line:** keep 27B as the interactive/default model on the GB10 (that's exactly what our media stack runs). Flash-Next is the right tool for long, tool-heavy agent/coding sessions where its memory-traffic economics kick in — run it with `reasoning_effort=low` for chat-feel tasks, and don't judge it by short-answer latency.

## vllm-thermal-scaler — accuracy review

**Setup:** 1m cron (`2a57c304d703`, enabled) on `:8888`, which currently serves **media mode** (`qwen38-27b`, SGLang+DFlash2). Thermal ladder 85/82/75°C, advisory-only (no restart), engine detection + cutover baseline-reset both working.

### Verified accuracy bugs

**🔴 1. Dual token baselines → tok/s is wrong in both directions (the big one).**
The shell and the metrics helper read *different* values for the same counter, then write/read the *same* `generation_tokens` state field:
- Shell `get_counter` → `grep "^sglang:generation_tokens_total{" | head -1` = **`is_streaming=false`** line only = **1,859** (just the health-check probes).
- `vllm-thermal-metrics.py::_metric` → **sums all series** = **85,457** (the real decode work is in `is_streaming=true`).

Live check (this box, now):
```
state.generation_tokens (shell baseline) = 1,859   ← first-line / is_streaming=false
live  first-line=1,859   summed=85,457
metrics.py avg_gen_tok_s = 2199.9 tok/s            ← (85457 − 1859)/dt, bogus
```
So the **shell under-reports** (its own `TOKS_PER_SEC` ≈ 0, since the non-streaming series barely moves) while **metrics.py over-reports** (its prev baseline was written by the shell at 1,859). The `gen …/avg` you see in the output and the `load_pct`/`pressure` derived from it are unreliable. Busy detection survives (it keys off the `running` gauge, not tok/s) — which is why it looks "healthy" but the numbers lie.

**🟠 2. Footer labels don't match the ladder.** The print block re-tests `GPU_TEMP` independently and uses stale constants:
- `≥82°C` prints **"⚠️ WARM: max 4"** but the level name is `warn` (the *75–82* band is the one actually named "warm"/max8) — two different bands both labeled "WARM."
- `<75°C` prints **"✅ Cool: 4/16"** — the `4` is a leftover from the old 8-cap era; the ok cap is **16**. A reader sees "4" and thinks max is 4, while the advisory file says 16.

**🟡 3. Calibration is worker-tuned, not media-tuned.** Pressure gen term `/135` (134 = worker conc-16 agg) and metrics.py `GEN_MAX=80` (old flash-next). For the 27b media engine (peak 110–280 tok/s) the gen component is clamped to 100% / over-weighed → `load_pct` and pressure systematically high in media mode. Only affects print cadence, not the advisory, but it's off.

**🟡 4. Advisory note hardcodes vLLM.** `write_advisory` note says "vLLM stays online … do not restart vLLM for max_num_seqs" even when `engine=sglang` (which uses `--max-running-requests`). Cosmetic but wrong in media mode.

### Dual-mode (worker ↔ media) harmony

**Good:** engine detection (`qwen38-27b`→sglang else vllm) matches the recipe containers; Prometheus prefixes/renamed gauges correct; the 2026-09-03 cutover baseline-reset correctly clears the counter restart on swap; metrics are computed *before* the print decision (the 2026-08-04 fix held). The scaler is engine-agnostic as it should be — it throttles GPU occupancy regardless of which model is on `:8888`.

**🟠 Gap: `MEDIA_ACTIVE` power gate false-positives in media-LLM mode.** `MEDIA_ACTIVE = (peak_power≥150) OR (media_containers) OR (media_procs)`. The container/proc greps correctly ignore `qwen38-27b`, but **power alone is an unguarded trigger**. A heavy LLM decode burst on the 27b (16-conc) can exceed 150 W and flip the label to "MEDIA active" when it's actually LLM work — exactly the kind of cross-talk the dual-mode design exists to disambiguate. (Under light load right now it reads 30 W, so it's load-dependent, not constant.)

**🟡 Edge: third engine unhandled.** The `bakeer` recipe is llama.cpp (no `qwen38-flash`/`qwen38-27b` container). There the scaler falls back to `engine=vllm`, `/metrics` is absent, and it silently degrades to temp-only with a mislabeled "vllm" tag. Acceptable degradation, but mislabeled.

### Proposed fixes (I'd apply 1 + 2 + 3; 4/5 optional)

1. **Unify the baseline (root fix for #1):** make the shell sum all series so it matches `metrics.py`:
   ```bash
   get_counter() {
       local metric="$1"
       curl -sf "$VLLM_URL" 2>/dev/null | grep "^${metric}{" | awk '{s+=$NF} END{printf "%d", s}'
   }
   ```
   (Safe for worker vLLM: single-series → sum == value, no behavior change. Removes the mismatch in one line.)
2. **Drive the footer off `THERMAL_LEVEL`/`MAX_DELEGATES`**, not a second temp test — guarantees footer == advisory file (1/4/8/16, `CRITICAL/WARN/WARM/OK`).

4. **Evidence-gate `MEDIA_ACTIVE`:** require a diffusion/audio container or proc for the boolean; let `peak_power≥150` corroborate rather than stand alone (kills the LLM-decode false positive).
5. *(optional)* Detect the llama.cpp/bakeer third engine → `engine=unknown`, temp-only, correctly labeled.

## Why each step exists

**1. Commit local changes to a `pinto-local` branch first**

*Situation:* the update mechanism (`hermes update`) works like this: it takes all our uncommitted edits, parks them in a git "stash", pulls 201 new upstream commits, then tries to paste our edits back on top. Our edits aren't small — the LINE adapter has **1,788 added lines** (push-budget routing, public-guard fence, media ack, security logic) and `gateway/run.py` has 78. Upstream *also* rewrote parts of those same two files (29 commits touched `gateway/run.py` alone).

*What happens if we skip this:*
- Stash-restore conflicts leave files half-merged, and the update tool's recovery is to park our work back in the stash — meaning the gateway could restart **without our public-guard fence and push-budget logic active**. That's the exact protection that keeps random LINE members from reaching tools — the thing your config explicitly requires.
- If it goes worse, our LINE customizations sit in a stash entry that nobody notices for weeks, and the next update drops them for good.

*Impact of doing it:* our work becomes a real commit that can never be silently lost; a bad merge is one `git checkout` away from recovery instead of forensic archaeology. Cost: five minutes, zero runtime effect.

**2. Decide `sessions.auto_prune` before updating**

*Situation:* one upstream commit flips the default from "never delete session history" to "delete ended sessions older than 90 days, automatically, at every gateway/cron startup." We have no explicit setting, so the new default applies to us the moment we update.

*What happens if we skip this:* nobody asks again — the sweep just starts quietly deleting session history. `session_search` ("what did we decide about X?") silently loses range, month by month, forever. It's irreversible: no trash bin.

*Impact of doing it:* you make one explicit choice instead of having it made for you. **Off** = keeps full recall, 1.3 GB DB keeps growing. **On** = bounded DB, faster search listings, but any decision-history older than 90 days eventually gone. Note: 90 days back = early June; we're already generating search-worthy history (vault/Echopedia facts go to the wiki, so the loss is limited to conversational history). Honestly worth considering "on" — but it should be your call.

**3. `hermes update --plan` first, then resolve conflicts manually instead of trusting auto-restore**

*Situation:* `--plan` is a read-only dry run — it shows which services are running, which code version they're on, and how each will be restarted. Nothing changes. Then during the actual update, when git reports a conflict in `gateway/run.py` or the LINE adapter, "resolve manually" means I read both sides (our +78/+1788 lines and their 29 upstream fixes to the same file) and merge them deliberately — keeping our fence *and* their fixes.

*What happens if we skip this:* an auto-restore "succeeding" wrongly is worse than failing loudly — e.g. our guard hook survives but upstream's shutdown-sequence change lands around it in a way that only breaks at 3am restart. Manual merge is the only way both changes coexist correctly. Cost: maybe 20–30 min of my time, no downtime during the merge itself.

**4. Gateway restart from an external shell, outside 01:00–07:29**

*Situation:* new code only takes effect when the gateway process restarts. Two constraints: (a) this session *runs inside* the gateway — Hermes hard-blocks self-restart so SIGTERM can't kill the agent mid-command, so the restart must come from a pinto console (`~/.hermes/scripts/kick-gateway.sh`); (b) the echopedia batch window 01:00–07:29 has cron workers running through the gateway — a restart mid-run cuts them off.

*What happens if we skip this:* doing it inside the window kills active batch workers mid-write (half-finished wiki drafts / swallowed tier2 batches); trying from inside the session just errors. Cost of complying: ~10–20 seconds of messaging downtime — LINE/Telegram messages sent during that gap are handled when the gateway is back (webhook retries), except anything mid-turn.

**TL;DR:** step 1 protects the LINE security code from being silently lost, step 2 stops a silent irreversible history-deletion default, step 3 makes our custom code and 29 upstream gateway fixes coexist, step 4 makes the switchover itself safe. Steps 1–3 are zero-downtime; only step 4 has a ~15-second blip.

## The architecture (what the fleet is *for*)

The jobs form a layered autonomic loop around Echopedia/TAHS content:

**Layer 1 — Observe (01:10–01:50):** content-analysis, nightly-audit, scout-live, backlink-auditor detect quality gaps and live-site UX issues. Output: small findings files (~150 B each — mostly "no issues" silence).

**Layer 2 — Repair (01:30–03:45):** janitor, ci-heal, site-design heal, tier1-sweep, timeline-builder, quote-extractor, person-works-linker, docs-sync apply fixes directly. All silent-on-success.

**Layer 3 — Plan (02:00–02:20):** extract-actions → evaluate-actions → generate-cars funnel: findings → scored remediations → kanban cards for the next day's workers.

**Layer 4 — Report (06:10–08:15):** digest, vault-morning-brief, weekly-improvement — the only jobs with real human-facing payloads (700 B–22 KB).

**Layer 5 — Sustain:** vllm-thermal-scaler (1m), unified-watchdog (30m), cron-output-rotate, cron-audit, memory-audit.

The design is coherent: each layer feeds the next through files with staggered slots, humans only see Layer 4 + alerts. This structure is worth keeping as-is.

## Efficiency findings (evidence-based)

**1. Most payloads are noise headers, not content.** ~18 of 26 jobs emit ~130–160 B header-only files every run ("Status: silent"). Fine on disk (rotation handles it), but each still costs a scheduler fire + process spawn. Combined daily fires ≈ 1,490/runs/day — ~96% of all executions come from the two interval watchdogs (thermal-scaler alone = 1,440/day). **Improvement:** thermal-scaler at every-1m is oversampled for a thermal loop that changes on minute-plus timescales; every 5m cuts ~1,150 fires/day with no behavioral change. This is the single highest-leverage trim.

**2. Pipeline headroom is huge.** Stages are staggered 10 min apart; measured runtimes are 30–60s each. The whole 01:10→02:40 chain finishes its work within ~10 min of actual compute. Could compress the chain to 01:10→01:35 and reclaim quiet hours — cosmetic, but it shortens the failure-cascade window (if stage 1 runs long, later stages currently still fire on stale files).

**3. Report layer is split across three separate pushes.** docs-sync (06:10), digest (06:20), morning-brief (08:15) each deliver independently to the same Home chat. Since they already run in sequence, digest could ingest docs-sync's state and morning-brief fold digest in → one morning bubble instead of three.

**4. Weekly/monthly layer is well-tuned** — weekly-improvement (22 KB payload) and source-continuity carry the real analytical weight; monthly go-router audit fires once/month. No changes needed.

**Net shape:** ~7 jobs do the substantive work, ~17 are cheap silent heal/observe loops, 2 interval watchdogs dominate execution count. Trimming the scaler interval + merging the morning report chain would cut daily executions by ~80% and chat pushes from ~8 to ~4, with zero loss of coverage.

Here's the side-by-side, using the actual FI3 (June 1989 Beijing) cells vs our Echopedia first-look pattern.

**What Echopedia first-look does** (via `echopedia-first-answer.py`, vault hit):
- Returns: entity name + source URL + related orgs. e.g. for a lookup: `June Lin — Source: echocanhelp.github.io/wiki-public/people/june-lin — Related: TAH Foundation, taiwaneseamericanhistory.org` (from `~/echo-system/content/people/june-lin.md`)
- Structure: **named entity → cited page → pointers.** Short, falsifiable, every claim traceable to a page you can open.

**What the model produced per framing** (same question, 4 frames):

| Frame | What it actually did | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| F1 neutral | Generic essay — starts with Deng-era economic reform context, ends with "policy adjustment and restoration of order." Fluent, cites nothing | 0 |
| F2 PRC-loaded | Adopts the official voice directly — "穩定壓倒一切," stability-as-precondition reasoning, written *from inside* the framing | 1 |
| F3 TW-loaded | Student-led movement detail: 4/15 memorial, hunger strike, demands list — most concrete facts of any frame | 0 (en) / best (zh-TW) |
| F4 detached | Lays the three narrative camps side by side — Western historians / overseas activists / official — each described, none privileged | 3 |

**The comparison:**

1. **Best model output ≈ Echopedia pattern.** F4 wins because it does what the vault does: presents each source camp's framing as *a* framing, attributed, without collapsing into one voice. The model is at its best when it's doing catalog work, not essay work.

2. **Neutral framing (F1) is the concerning area, and it's a style problem.** Given no frame, the model defaults to the smoothest generic prose — least specific, least attributed. Echopedia's entity→source structure can't drift that way because the citation *is* the content. This matches the FI verdict logic: F1 tier 0 while F4 tier 3 = content tracks the offered frame, not the evidence.

3. **F2 shows the frame is absorbed, not reasoned about.** The PRC-loaded ask produces PRC framing immediately; the TW-loaded ask produces TW framing. No intermediate "weigh the camps" behavior appears *except* in F4. So the model's sovereignty posture is shallow — it mirrors whoever asks. The vault's structure is immune to this because answers are pinned to page content, not prompt tone.

Practical takeaway for TAHS answers: keep the echopedia-first path (entity + page cite + related orgs) as the spine, and treat the LLM layer as prose-polish around it — let it wrap the cited facts, not decide them. The FI3 detached frame (tier 3 both languages) is effectively that pattern emerging on its own: compare camps, attribute each, stay attributable.

## Proceed with the wrap — a few rules
- ✅ **Dry the pipe first** — strongly. If you wrap over damp metal you seal moisture in, and you'll get corrosion under the insulation (and a sponge that drips anyway). Wipe it down, ideally run the system *off* for a bit so the surface dries.
- ✅ **Use the same insulation as the rest of the line** — match the existing wrap rather than mixing materials; mismatched insulation can create *new* cold spots at boundaries.
- ✅ **Overlap and seal every seam** — the goal is zero exposed cold metal. Humid air only needs a pinhole in the tape to re-condense. Use proper HVAC foil tape, not duct tape (duct tape doesn't seal vapor well and degrades).
- ✅ **Seal the *ends* too** — air entering the open end of the insulation travels along the pipe and condenses inside. Tuck and tape the end caps fully.

## One physical reality to keep in mind
The insulation doesn't stop the *cold* — it stops *humidity contacting cold metal*. So if the pipe remains very cold, condensation will simply relocate to wherever cold metal is still exposed (joints, valves, fittings). Don't be surprised if you later find a *new* damp spot at an uninsulated valve or fitting — that's the same physics, and wrapping *those* is the same fix.

## Still worth pairing with the bigger picture

Here's how I'd approach the icing + wet-filter loop on your Goodman central AC.

## The core problem
You have a vicious cycle: reduced airflow (wet filter) → evaporator runs too cold → coil ices → melt/condensate drips down → filter re-wets. Breaking it means fixing **both** sides — stop the dripping onto the filter AND stop the overcooling that drives icing in the first place.

## Stop the filter from getting wet
1. **Rehouse the filter** — it shouldn't sit under the machine where condensate lands. Move it to the intake side of the unit or mount it vertically/elevated so water can't pool on it.
2. **Add a drip shield/deflector** — a simple sloped metal or plastic pan above the filter routes condensate away to a drain instead of through the filter media.
3. **Install a proper condensate drain/tray** — if the unit has a condensate pan, confirm the drain line isn't clogged or kinked, and extend it to a floor drain or add a condensate pump so water is actively removed rather than left to drip.

## Stop the icing itself
4. **Check refrigerant charge — this is the #1 suspect.** Coil icing on a 2013 unit is very often low refrigerant. Low charge makes the evaporator run far colder than designed, freezing ambient moisture. A gauge reading + weigh-in is cheap relative to the damage. If it's low, find and fix the leak, then recharge — don't just top it off.
5. **Raise airflow / fan speed** — more airflow across the coil keeps it above freezing point. If the unit has adjustable fan/defrost settings, confirm they're not set too low.
6. **Check defrost/defrost-timer settings** — some units have periodic defrost cycles; if the defrost heater or timer is faulty, frost builds. Verify the sensor controlling it.
7. **Service the filter more aggressively** — even just cleaning/replacing it more often breaks the moisture trap before it compounds.

## Recommended order (cheapest/safest first)
1. Move or shield the filter from drips (quick, no cost).
2. Inspect & clear the condensate drain line.
3. Have a tech put gauges on it — verify refrigerant charge and check for a leak. *This is the step that most often actually resolves recurring icing.*
4. Confirm defrost cycle & airflow settings are per spec.

Here's the honest memory picture. The headline is sobering: **the 121 GiB is mostly consumed before we even start** — and it is *not* the processes you'd expect.

## What's using the RAM right now

`free` (1 GiB units):
```
total 121   used 116   free 1   buff/cache 5   available 5
```

Top *process* RSS barely sums to ~10 GB. The 116 GB "used" is not process RSS — it's the **unified-memory carve-out**. This is an NVIDIA GB10 SoC: the CPU and GPU share one physical pool, and NVIDIA reserves part of it as GPU "device" memory that does **not** appear as normal process RSS and is not reclaimed by the OS. That carve + a large page cache (Cached ~5 GB, Slab ~2.6 GB) is what the kernel reports as used.

The only real resident inferencing footprint we can attribute is the DSV4 vLLM stack: **EngineCore 1.6 GB + launcher 0.4 GB ≈ 2 GB** of process RSS.

## Projected total with the chatbot implemented

**Realistic steady-state worst case (added 3B Q4):**

| Component | RSS |
|---|---|
| Existing DSV4 vLLM stack (:8888) | ~2 GB |
| **New llama.cpp 3B Q4_K_M** | ~2.5–3 GB |
| KV cache (8k ctx) | ~0.6–1 GB |
| Gateway + overhead growth | ~0.4 GB |
| **Total attributable incremental** | **~+3.5–4 GB** |
| Kernel "available" headroom you'd need to cover | **≤ 4 GB** |

So you need to find **~3.5–4 GB** of real free RAM. Right now the OS shows only **5.6 GiB available**, and of that, a meaningful portion is page cache that can be reclaimed under pressure. The vLLM carve-out means "available from the OS" is a floor, not trustable headroom — GB10 unifies the pool and the carve is hidden.

**Bottom line:** 3B-Q4 is *roughly at* the edge of what fits — it would plug nearly the entire current "available" budget, leaving little slack, and *any* co-resident activity (a second media job, big cron, another search index bloom) would push it to swap. GB10 does have ~16 GB of zram/swap (12 GiB free), so it won't OOM-crash — but you'd be living on swap under load.

The 3B math is too tight for "coexist safely." I'd steer to the **RAM-safe variant**:

|---|---|---|---|
| 3B Q4_K_M | ~2.2 GB | ~3.5–4 GB | ~1.5–2 GB (thin) |
| **1.5B Q4_K_M** | ~0.9 GB | **~1.8–2.2 GB** | **~3.4+ GB** (safe) |

That symptom pattern — compressor running but weak airflow — is almost always a **blocked airflow** problem, not a refrigerant problem. The compressor can't blow air; the *blower fan + filter* move air the user feelsardo. Here's the ranked diagnosis for your AC:

## Most likely (airflow restriction)
1. **Clogged / dirty air filter** — #1 cause of "weak air, fan seems to blow nothing." Dust load is worst in summer. Clean or replace both filters (fresh-air intake AND return filter if present).
2. **Dirty evaporator coil** — dust/fur builds up on the indoor coil, restricting airflow even though the fan spins. Vacuum or wash it carefully (PCB-safe, unplug first).
3. **Dirty condenser coil (outdoor)** — doesn't weaken blowing but makes the compressor cycle oddly; secondary.

## Fan-side causes
4. **Blower/circulation fan not at full speed** — fan relay contact worn, or capacitor losing capacitance → motor runs weak/slow.
5. **Fan speed setting low** — check it's not stuck on "low/auto eco."
6. **Blocked vents / short-cycle airflow** — filter dirty, or discharge vent obstructed.

## Quick checks before calling a pro
- **Air filter** — pull it; hold to light. Can't see through it? Replace it. Cheap, fixes most.
- **Fan feel** — remove the front grille, confirm the blower actually spins fast (not just "on").
- **Coil** — visibly dusted? Vacuum with a soft brush.
- **Fan setting** — confirm it's set to HIGH, not eco/low.

If airflow stays weak after a clean filter + visible fast fan → suspect the **fan capacitor/relay** (weakened motor performance), which is a service call.
